A metal detectorist found a Viking sword and rare oval brooches on the Isle of Man, and his father had helped find the island’s only other pair

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (918 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, daniel Crowe found a Viking sword, oval brooches and trading weights over 1,100 years old on the Isle of Man.
  • A metal detectorist on the Isle of Man has found a Viking sword, a set of bronze brooches and trading weights and scales, all more than 1,100 years old.
  • The finder, Daniel Crowe, is not the first in his family to make a discovery like this.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, daniel Crowe found a Viking sword, oval brooches and trading weights over 1,100 years old on the Isle of Man. His father helped find the island's only other pair.

A metal detectorist on the Isle of Man has found a Viking sword, a set of bronze brooches and trading weights and scales, all more than 1,100 years old. The objects are believed to come from a double Viking burial.

The finder, Daniel Crowe, is not the first in his family to make a discovery like this. In December 2018, his father, John Crowe, and fellow detectorist Craig Evans found the only other pair of Viking oval brooches ever discovered on the island.

Sources indicate that the latest collection was declared Treasure by the Isle of Man Coroner for Inquests, and Manx National Heritage revealed it on November 9. Part of it went on display at the Manx Museum in Douglas two days later.

The finds date to around AD 900. Besides the sword, the haul includes three bronze brooches, decorated lead weights, fragments of bronze balance scales, a bronze ladle and an axehead.

Industry observers note that fellow detectorist Rhett Britton helped with the search. He found the axehead, part of the scales and other iron objects.

The sword is the thirteenth Viking sword found on the island. About two-thirds of it survives. X-rays revealed fine silver inlay and twisted silver wire on parts of its hilt, and only two other Manx Viking swords carry comparable decoration.

It is broken, probably on purpose as part of the burial ritual. Some more damage happened later, while it lay in the ground.

It has been revealed that two of the brooches are oval and decorated with interlocking animals, a distinctive feature of Viking art. Brooches like these were usually worn by women.

The pair found by John Crowe and Craig Evans in 2018 dates to around AD 900 to 950. The new pair could be about 50 years older, which would make it potential evidence of the earliest known female Viking Age burial on the Isle of Man.

Oval brooches were particularly common in the Viking homelands and are seen almost as national dress.

In 2020, Manx National Heritage mentioned their absence from the island until the 2018 find had led to theories that only men from Scandinavia settled there in the early Viking Age.

Recent findings suggest that the third brooch was originally gilded. It has spiral decoration and a glass center, and it is the first of its kind found on the island.

In a recent development, jewelry typically associated with women, found alongside a sword traditionally associated with men, raises a possibility. The objects may come from a double burial, or from separate graves of the same period.

The site was disturbed at some point over the last thousand years, so the exact circumstances are still uncertain.

At the site of the 2018 brooches, archaeologists from York Archaeological Trust carried out a small excavation but found no grave.

Industry observers note that the decorated lead weights and bronze scales would have been used to weigh precious metals and coins during trade. The weights are the first of their type found on the Isle of Man.

Silver and coins also turn up in hoards across the Viking world, like a buried 10th-century hoard that revealed vast Viking trade networks.

One weight carries a bronze fitting, possibly taken from a small chest or a religious object. Its art style is typical of Britain and Ireland at the time, which suggests the settlers reused objects from other cultures.

The ladle, perhaps used at feasts or ceremonies, is another type of object never recorded before on the island.

“This is an extraordinary discovery and one of the most significant groups of Viking Age objects found on the Isle of Man,” said Allison Fox, Curator for Archaeology at Manx National Heritage.

Sources indicate that crowe chose not to clean the objects and handed them over in the state they came out of the ground. That kept traces of evidence that could otherwise have been lost.

His father and Evans did the same in 2018. In 2020, Fox remarked this mattered because the brooches were fragile and small fragments of textiles from the clothes the woman was buried in might still survive.

In a recent development, this time, before conservation began, the radiology team at Manx Care scanned the objects. The scans looked beneath layers of compacted soil and guided the conservator in uncovering and preserving the objects.

Detectorists elsewhere have made similar finds, such as the hiker with a metal detector who found a Viking treasure hoard and the detectorist who found Finland’s largest Viking Age silver hoard.

Recent findings suggest that manx National Heritage has not said exactly where the objects were found, only that the landowner cooperated. It also has not given a date for the discovery.

Industry observers note that conservation and research are still underway, and they may reveal more about who owned these objects. Several of them are the first of their kind on the island, so they offer a rare look at early Viking settlement, burial and daily life there.

Visitors can see a selection of the finds in the Viking Gallery of the Manx Museum.

The information was obtained from Manx National Heritage and its 2020 announcement on the earlier brooches.

Latest Update: November’s full moon on Nov. 24 is the first of three supermoons in a row, and it will pass close to the Pleiades

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The November 24, 2026 Beaver Moon will be the first of three consecutive supermoons, with views of the Pleiades, Mars and Jupiter before dawn.
  • The full Moon of November 24, 2026, will be a supermoon, the first of three consecutive supermoons that run through January.
  • That is midmorning on the East Coast, so the best views come before dawn and again that evening.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The November 24, 2026 Beaver Moon will be the first of three consecutive supermoons, with views of the Pleiades, Mars and Jupiter before dawn.

The full Moon of November 24, 2026, will be a supermoon, the first of three consecutive supermoons that run through January.

The Moon turns full at 9:53 a.m. EST (14:53 UT), the U.S. Naval Observatory calculates. That is midmorning on the East Coast, so the best views come before dawn and again that evening.

Before sunrise, the nearly full Moon will pass close to the Pleiades star cluster, while Mars and Jupiter shine in another part of the sky.

In a recent development, the Moon’s orbit is slightly oval, so its distance from Earth changes. At its closest point, called perigee, it is about 226,000 miles (363,300 kilometers) away, and at its farthest about 251,000 miles (405,500 kilometers).

It has been revealed that A supermoon occurs when a full Moon coincides with that closest approach, NASA explains. The word is not an official astronomical term and typically describes a full Moon within at least 90 percent of perigee.

Such a Moon can appear up to 14 percent bigger and 30 percent brighter than the faintest full Moon of the year.

It has been revealed that “It might be hard to detect a supermoon visually, but it does have an effect on Earth,” the space agency’s page states. A Moon at perigee can cause higher tides than usual.

Measured against an average full Moon, the gain is smaller: up to 7 percent larger and 15 percent brighter, the Royal Observatory Greenwich notes.

When it turns full, the Moon will be roughly 224,200 miles (360,800 kilometers) from Earth. That is around 12,400 miles (20,000 kilometers) closer than average, by the Greenwich astronomers’ figures.

Perigee itself arrives about 30 hours later, on November 25 at 4:01 p.m. EST. The Moon will then be 223,400 miles (359,567 kilometers) away, a government almanac from Land Information Newly introduced Zealand demonstrates.

In a recent development, december’s full Moon falls on December 23 at 8:28 p.m. EST. Perigee follows about seven hours later at 221,800 miles (356,903 kilometers), the closest of the three.

The third full Moon comes on January 22, 2027, at 7:17 a.m. EST. Perigee occurs the previous afternoon, at 222,200 miles (357,530 kilometers).

It has been revealed that measured at perigee, November’s supermoon is therefore the most distant of the trio. It follows the Beaver Moon of November 2025.

U.S. Naval Observatory rise and set tables put moonset in Upcoming York at 7:05 a.m. EST, 12 minutes after sunrise. In Los Angeles, the Moon sets at 6:49 a.m. PST.

Early risers should look low in the west, toward Taurus, the constellation that holds the Pleiades.

Recent findings suggest that the International Occultation Timing Association lists that date among the Moon’s 2026 passages over the cluster. In an occultation, the Moon moves in front of a star and hides it.

Sources indicate that the listing does not rank it among the year’s best passages. Bright moonlight will also make the cluster’s faint stars harder to pick out.

Higher up, Mars and Jupiter have been neighbors all month. They appeared about 1.2 degrees apart on the mornings of November 15 and 16, slightly more than two full Moon widths.

Jupiter is the brighter of the two, and Mars has a reddish tint. Binoculars or a low-powered telescope, under 40x magnification, give a closer look.

The planets have since drifted apart and stand high in the south before dawn, near Regulus, the brightest star in Leo.

In a recent development, such Mars and Jupiter pairings recur every 2 to 2.5 years on average, by the Royal Observatory’s count. Mars circles the Sun faster and laps Jupiter in the night sky.

The second chance comes at dusk. “Look east around sunset to watch it rise,” NASA’s November skywatching guide advises.

“It may look even bigger near the horizon, but that’s the Moon illusion,” the guide adds. The effect is common to any full Moon.

Sources indicate that moonrise in New York is at 4:16 p.m. EST, 16 minutes before sunset. Los Angeles sees the Moon come up at 4:43 p.m. PST, two minutes ahead of the Sun’s setting.

Bill Ingalls, then NASA’s senior photographer, shared supermoon photography tips in 2016.

“Don’t make the mistake of photographing the moon by itself with no reference to anything,” Ingalls mentioned. “I’ve certainly done it myself, but everyone will get that shot.”.

In a recent development, he suggested including a local landmark to give a photo a sense of place. For phone cameras, he advised holding a finger on the Moon to lock focus, then sliding it to adjust exposure.

In a recent development, beaver Moon is a nickname for November’s full Moon. The name draws on several traditions and folklore in Native American and European culture.

In a recent development, one explanation is that beavers spend November fortifying their dams and stocking food for winter. The month was also the season to trap the animals for their thick, winter-ready pelts.

“There is disagreement over the origin of November’s ‘Beaver Moon’ name,” the Royal Observatory’s monthly highlights state.

The word “supermoon” was coined in 1979, the same 2024 NASA post indicates.

The information was obtained from NASA’s skywatching guide.

Industry News: Nov. 21, 1993: The death of Bruno Rossi

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that born in Venice, Italy, in 1905, Bruno Rossi attended the University of Bologna, graduating with a doctorate in physics in 1927.
  • Throughout his long career across countries and institutions, Rossi laid the groundwork for the study of several key fields in astronomy and astrophysics.
  • Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

Sources indicate that born in Venice, Italy, in 1905, Bruno Rossi attended the University of Bologna, graduating with a doctorate in physics in 1927. When race-based laws inspired by his country’s growing closeness with Nazi Germany meant the Jewish Rossi had to leave Italy, he made his way to the U.S. In 1940, Rossi became an associate professor of physics at Cornell University, and from 1943-1946, he worked on the Manhattan Project at Los Alamos Laboratory. After the war, Rossi joined the faculty of MIT, where he remained until his retirement in the early ’70s.

Throughout his long career across countries and institutions, Rossi laid the groundwork for the study of several key fields in astronomy and astrophysics. His research into cosmic rays became the basis of high-energy particle physics, while his pioneering search for cosmic X-rays jump-started X-ray astronomy. Rossi also conducted trailblazing research into the interplanetary medium, and contributed to the development of public policy for space exploration. Rossi passed away at age 88 on Nov. 21, 1993. Today, among other honors and memorials that Rossi accrued, the Bruno B. Rossi Prize for astrophysics is awarded yearly.

Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

Industry News: Some allergies may start in a part of the body that is meant to protect us

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1523 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A latest review explores whether trouble clearing damaged mitochondria in the body’s protective cells could help set off some allergic diseases.
  • Sources indicate that A patch of skin may look perfectly healthy in someone with eczema.
  • An analysis of gene activity in the skin of eczema patients, in patches that showed no rash at all, found unusual activity in two sets of genes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A latest review explores whether trouble clearing damaged mitochondria in the body’s protective cells could help set off some allergic diseases.

Sources indicate that A patch of skin may look perfectly healthy in someone with eczema. No redness, no itching, no obvious sign of trouble. Yet inside the cells, changes may already be taking place.

An analysis of gene activity in the skin of eczema patients, in patches that showed no rash at all, found unusual activity in two sets of genes.

These were genes involved in maintaining the skin barrier and in protecting skin cells against chemical damage.

Recent findings suggest that A finding like that leads to a newly introduced question. What if changes in the body’s protective barriers help set off allergic inflammation?

A newly introduced review suggests that mitochondria, the tiny structures inside our cells that help produce energy, could play a role in how some allergic diseases develop.

The cells that line our skin, gut, nose and airways all need that energy to form a protective barrier.

The authors propose that when barrier cells struggle to clear damaged mitochondria, they may send signals that trigger inflammation.

The team was led by Peter Smith, a clinical immunologist at Griffith University in Australia, and included researchers from the United States, Belgium, Ireland, Scotland, Switzerland and Singapore.

Of course, the fresh review doesn’t solve the allergy problem. Smith stated the team was clear that the idea is a hypothesis which has yet to be tested, and not a settled mechanism.

“For 60 years, we’ve taught that allergies start with the immune system and the barrier breaks as a consequence, but our work suggests it may be the other way around,” Smith stated.

There was already a substantial amount of published data that the researchers could use to look for patterns in the gene activity of patients with allergic disease.

A total of 116 comparisons, covering 3,776 patients with allergic disease and 2,164 healthy controls, were brought together for the review by Smith and his colleagues. Smith said it was the largest collection of its kind that the team was aware of.

A list of 350 genes, involved in 19 different aspects of mitochondrial function and barrier integrity, was fixed in advance, before any of the data had been examined.

There were seven different types of tissue analyzed in the review, which generated 212 separate estimates. After correction for the number of comparisons that had been made, nine of those 212 estimates remained significant.

The majority of those nine findings came from the data of patients with eosinophilic esophagitis, a disease in which immune cells build up in the esophagus.

This is the tube that carries food from the mouth down to the stomach.

Within healthy cells, worn-out mitochondria are constantly broken down by the cell’s own cleanup machinery, and their parts are recycled.

In the patients with this disease, the genes for that cleanup process were less active, and this was the case in all 13 of the independent patient groups.

The finding applied to two genes that are central to the removal of damaged mitochondria, both of which were reduced in every group. A third gene, which is involved in adapting to low oxygen levels, was also less active in all 13 groups.

It is the consistency of the result that the authors rely on.

It has been revealed that the 13 groups had been assembled by different laboratories. Yet all 13 pointed in the same direction.

Eczema was examined in the same review, including in skin from patients that appeared to be normal.

Although eczema is an itchy inflammatory skin disease, the samples in one series were taken from skin that indicated no signs of inflammation.

Even in skin without a visible rash, a gene that dampens the cell’s antioxidant response was more active.

Genes for two proteins that help seal the skin, filaggrin and claudin-1, were less active.

The analysis found no broad drop in mitochondrial gene activity in those samples, which came from people who already had eczema.

The signature did not turn up in every allergic disease, and the authors are direct about that.

In a recent development, it was missing in established asthma and in nasal polyps. In hay fever, it was only partly present.

According to recent reports, airway samples from people with asthma make the point. There, the mitochondrial measures came out at background level.

They were two to five times smaller than the immune signal in the same tissue.

Psoriasis adds a second caution, because it is inflammatory but not allergic. Inflamed psoriasis skin carried a mitochondrial deficit of similar depth, the authors wrote.

So the fault is not unique to allergy.

Industry observers note that rather than explain these results away, the authors treat asthma as the limit of their idea. They call it the exception that bounds the model.

Scientists have hunted for allergy genes for about three decades. In all that time, no genome-wide study has implicated the mitochondrial genome or the genes that control it.

The authors read that silence as a design problem, not as an absence.

The genotyping chips used by the founding allergy studies barely carry any mitochondrial DNA.

Industry observers note that other events in the model would be invisible to DNA analysis altogether. They are chemical changes to proteins, the authors wrote, which leave no DNA variant behind.

Recent findings suggest that single-cell methods add another blind spot. Cells with high mitochondrial readings are routinely discarded as dying, and those are the very cells in question.

Most genome-wide work sampled blood, while the proposed fault sits in the lining tissue.

What those studies did recover were genes like filaggrin, which builds the skin barrier. Genes that run the immune response were recovered as well.

Every one belongs to a layer the old model was built to find.

The largest synthesis of food allergy risk to date pooled 190 studies from 40 countries. It covered 2.8 million participants and returned 342 separate risk factors.

A list that long isn’t a mechanism, the authors wrote. It is what a field produces when its associations have no single meeting place.

Smith’s team nominates one. The review names 19 modern exposures that may act on the same target.

The authors propose that these exposures may affect how mitochondria work in barrier cells.

In a recent development, among the 19 are ultra-processed food, emulsifiers, microplastics and air pollution. Caesarean delivery, loss of dietary fiber and early antibiotics are also listed.

For now, that convergence is an argument rather than a demonstrated mechanism.

Recent findings suggest that not every exposure pushes toward allergy. Some appear to protect against it.

Children raised on traditional cattle farms develop 50% to 60% less asthma, hay fever and allergic sensitization.

The review reads that protection through the same handful of genes. Four separate protective signals were traced back to them, the authors wrote.

In a recent development, fiber may work the same way. Fiber feeds gut microbes, which produce compounds that fuel the cells lining the gut.

Industry observers note that the review has an notable limitation. All the samples came from people who already had an allergic disease, so researchers could not tell what happened before it began.

In a recent development, inflammation can change how cells use energy. This means the researchers could not determine whether mitochondrial problems caused the inflammation or developed afterward.

Recent findings suggest that the data also demonstrated only how active certain genes were. They did not directly measure how much energy mitochondria produced, how they used oxygen or how promptly they recycled damaged parts.

Smith holds a provisional patent application related to diagnosing and treating the problems described in the review.

Sources indicate that the team also used a specially designed AI system to analyze the data. The researchers had chosen which genes to study before examining the results.

Nic West, a molecular immunologist at Griffith University’s School of Pharmacy and Medical Sciences, said the research also helps to explain why allergies can relapse.

“Today’s drugs act downstream, so the disease often returns when treatment stops as they do not reach the root cause,” West said.

The authors describe five findings that would refute their explanation if they were made, and they describe the one experiment that would settle its central claim.

“The next step is to measure these cells directly in infants before the allergy develops,” Smith noted.

This would involve following babies from birth, taking samples of their barrier cells, and then following the children to see whether or not they develop an allergy.

If the cells turn out to be normal at birth in the babies who go on to develop allergic disease, then the proposal fails.

It has been revealed that no study of that kind has yet been carried out. For now, the changes that have been found in the cells of the body’s barriers remain a proposal about where to look.

The full study was published in the journal Allergy.

Industry News: An invasive hornet that hunts honeybees was first found in the U.S. in 2023 and has since reached North Carolina

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The invasive yellow-legged hornet has spread to Georgia, South Carolina and North Carolina, threatening honeybees as nest numbers continue to rise.
  • It has been revealed that the yellow-legged hornet (Vespa velutina), an invasive predator of honeybees, has now been detected in three U.S.
  • North Carolina confirmed its first established presence on July 27, 2026, in Matthews, the North Carolina Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services announced.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The invasive yellow-legged hornet has spread to Georgia, South Carolina and North Carolina, threatening honeybees as nest numbers continue to rise.

It has been revealed that the yellow-legged hornet (Vespa velutina), an invasive predator of honeybees, has now been detected in three U.S. states: Georgia, South Carolina and North Carolina.

North Carolina confirmed its first established presence on July 27, 2026, in Matthews, the North Carolina Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services announced.

Sources indicate that the hornets were reported by a homeowner in Union County, North Carolina, who noticed suspicious activity at her hummingbird feeder. More than 200 survey traps were then set around her home to target the nest.

A beekeeper in Savannah, Georgia, found an unusual hornet on his property and reported it to state officials. On August 9, 2023, federal officials confirmed the identification.

It was the first time a live specimen of the species had been detected in the open United States, the Georgia Department of Agriculture states. The first nest, about 85 feet (26 meters) up a tree in a residential area, was eradicated within two weeks of that confirmation.

Sources indicate that south Carolina’s first known detection came on November 9, 2023. In spring 2024, several queens and one early-stage nest were found in Beaufort County, according to Clemson University‘s Department of Plant Industry.

In December 2025, a nest was found in York County, South Carolina, just south of the Charlotte metropolitan area. It was the first known nest outside the state’s Lowcountry.

According to recent reports, “This detection prompted us to ramp up surveillance this year in southern Union and Mecklenburg counties,” said Dr. Bill Foote, director of the North Carolina agency’s Plant Industry Division.

The North Carolina nest was “located and eliminated rapidly,” NC State Extension wrote on August 7. A separate confirmed case had by then developed in High Point.

The species is native to tropical and subtropical areas of Southeast Asia. Adults are 0.75 to 1 inch (1.9 to 2.5 centimeters) long, with a mostly dark body, a banded abdomen and distinct yellow legs.

In a recent development, yellow-legged hornets hover near the entrances of honeybee hives, a behavior called hawking. They pick off workers returning from foraging flights in midair.

Because the hornets attack honeybees, they can cause reduced foraging and colony failure, according to Don Hopkins, North Carolina’s state apiarist.

“This would result in reduced honey and other honeybee products, reduced crop production due to decreased pollination by honeybees and native pollinators, making the hornet a serious threat to North Carolina’s beekeeping community,” Hopkins added.

A 2019 study in Western Europe reported evidence of homing failures among foraging bees and of “foraging paralysis” in colonies with hornets at their entrances. Its simulations pointed to that paralysis as an notable mechanism underlying winter colony collapse.

Georgia’s Yellow-Legged Ledger of October 22, 2026, lists five nests for 2023, 47 for 2024 and 63 for 2025.

For 2026, the bulletin counts 144 nests found by that date, for a total of 259 since the first detection.

In South Carolina, 643 Lowcountry nests had been removed or scheduled for removal in 2026 as of October 26. Seven more were removed in the Upstate and Midlands.

That month, the first nests in Anderson and Kershaw counties were discovered and removed. Clemson’s program had 4,336 traps set across 14 South Carolina counties.

In a recent development, the hornet builds egg-shaped paper nests above the ground, often in trees. Nests can hold up to 6,000 workers and last a single year.

Recent findings suggest that late-season nests usually sit at least 33 feet (10 meters) above the ground. In November, most of the colony dies, and only newly produced queens survive to lie dormant from December to March.

In spring, each queen starts a nest about the size of a tennis ball.

The hornet moves to new areas primarily through human activities such as trade, travel and tourism. In Europe, where it is known as the Asian hornet, the species has been established since 2004.

“The genetics indicate it’s not from the European population,” stated Lewis Bartlett, an assistant professor at the University of Georgia, of the U.S. hornets. “It likely came directly from its native range in Asia.”.

Industry observers note that on April 30, 2026, a grain inspector photographed a live hornet on a vessel at the Port of Vancouver in Washington. State entomologists agreed it appeared to be a yellow-legged hornet, the Washington State Department of Agriculture reported.

Federal guidance is to never disturb a hornet or a potential nest. Residents should take a photo only if it is safe and record the exact location.

Only state or federal responders should remove nests. Attempting removal is dangerous and may help the hornet spread if the queen escapes.

The insect can be confused with other common wasps and hornets, including the northern giant hornet.

“When in doubt, point it out,” stated Jamie Ellis, director of the University of Georgia Bee Program.

In North Carolina, homemade traps should be set in March to catch new queens, in May to catch workers, or both. Trapping can continue until the first frost in the fall.

The information was obtained from the USDA Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service.

Republicans tap Moreno and Jack to lead Senate and House campaign arms

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bernie Moreno will chair the National Republican Senatorial Committee during the 2028 cycle.
  • Recent findings suggest that house and Senate Republicans picked their new campaign chiefs Tuesday, tasking Ohio Sen.
  • In their newly introduced positions, both will spearhead Republicans’ push to win back majorities on Capitol Hill after Democrats seized control of both chambers of Congress by flipping more than 40 House seats and at least seven Senate seats in last week’s midterm elections.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno will chair the National Republican Senatorial Committee during the 2028 cycle. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call file photo).

Recent findings suggest that house and Senate Republicans picked their new campaign chiefs Tuesday, tasking Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno and Georgia Rep. Brian Jack with leading the GOP campaign arms for the 2028 election cycle.

In their newly introduced positions, both will spearhead Republicans’ push to win back majorities on Capitol Hill after Democrats seized control of both chambers of Congress by flipping more than 40 House seats and at least seven Senate seats in last week’s midterm elections.

According to recent reports, republicans returned to Capitol Hill this week still reeling from their losses but resisted calls to delay Tuesday’s leadership elections. In the Senate, South Dakota’s John Thune was reelected Republican leader without any opposition, while Ohio Rep. Jim Jordan defeated Louisiana Rep. Steve Scalise in a closed-door, secret-ballot election to lead House Republicans next year.

Moreno will succeed South Carolina Sen. Tim Scott as chair of the National Republican Senatorial Committee.

“Republicans must enter this next election clear-eyed: the road ahead back to a Republican Senate majority will by no means be easy but the fight has never been so important,” the Ohio senator mentioned in a statement.

Speaking to reporters on Capitol Hill, Moreno described his upcoming role as “a hell of a job.” He remarked Republicans would be “absolute savages” on ending government corruption and continuing “to work for the American people.”.

“I suspect the best tailwind we’ll have is that the Democrats will learn all the wrong lessons,” he told reporters.

Industry observers note that moreno, a close ally of President Donald Trump, is currently serving his first term. He first ran for Senate during the 2022 cycle but dropped out of a crowded GOP primary eventually won by JD Vance. Two years later, buoyed by an endorsement from Trump, he won a contested primary for the state’s other Senate seat and went on to oust Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown that fall.

Brown is poised to return to the Senate after defeating appointed Republican Sen. Jon Husted last week in a special election for the remaining Senate term of Vice President Vance. While Ohio has swung heavily toward Republicans over the past decade, Democrats scored significant wins in the Buckeye State last week, winning several statewide offices and flipping three seats in the U.S. House.

But assuming he runs again for a full term, Brown will be on the ballot in 2028, setting up what’s likely to be a tense home-state fight.

In an apparent reference to the returning Brown, Moreno offered some Washington advice Tuesday: “Make sure you rent. Do not buy.”.

The 2028 Senate map gives Republican pickup opportunities in a handful of swing states, including Arizona, Georgia, Nevada, New Hampshire and Pennsylvania. The party will also be defending battleground seats in Alaska, Iowa, North Carolina and Wisconsin. Also on the Senate ballot are races for Republican-held seats in Kansas and South Carolina, where Democrats scored surprise wins last week.

Recent findings suggest that on the House side, Jack defeated Indiana Rep. Rudy Yakym III to become the next chairman of the National Republican Congressional Committee. He takes office after one of the worst elections for the GOP in recent decades and will succeed outgoing NRCC Chair Richard Hudson, who lost his own North Carolina seat last week.

House Republicans face the tough task of cutting into Democrats’ 40-plus-seat majority next cycle. But the party will have a slew of pickup opportunities, given the sheer number of seats Democrats won in historically red territory this year.

It has been revealed that like Moreno, Jack was first elected to Congress 2024, leveraging a close relationship with Trump to win an open seat outside Atlanta. He previously was White House director of political affairs during Trump’s first term and was a senior adviser to the president’s 2024 campaign. Over the past two years, he served as the NRCC’s recruitment chair.

Savannah Behrmann contributed to this report.

Latest Update: Teens who eat more junk food may have more mental health and behavior problems

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1571 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A review of 17 Australian studies linked diets high in fried foods, sweets and sugary drinks to poorer teen mental health and lower scores on some school tests.
  • Australian teenagers who more often ate fried foods and sweets and drank sugary drinks tended to have more mental health or behavioral problems.
  • According to recent reports, A review of 17 Australian studies also linked similar eating patterns to lower scores on some school tests.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A review of 17 Australian studies linked diets high in fried foods, sweets and sugary drinks to poorer teen mental health and lower scores on some school tests.

Australian teenagers who more often ate fried foods and sweets and drank sugary drinks tended to have more mental health or behavioral problems.

According to recent reports, A review of 17 Australian studies also linked similar eating patterns to lower scores on some school tests. Findings on body weight were mixed.

Yet sugary drinks and other high-calorie, low-nutrient foods are known to contribute to excess weight in children.

In a recent development, the studies were gathered in a latest review. Its first author is Zegeye Abebe Abitew, a research associate at Flinders University in Adelaide.

The senior author is Yohannes Melaku, an associate professor at the Flinders Health and Medical Research Institute.

Food that packs many calories into a small serving is described by researchers as energy-dense.

“In these vital formative years of children’s growth and development, there are clear benefits of following a healthy diet high in fruit, veg, whole grains and fish compared to eating too many ‘energy dense’ fatty, sweet and highly processed grains, red meat and other foods,” Melaku noted.

Industry observers note that according to the authors, the findings add to the case for programs that promote healthy eating from early in life. The links were also described by them as suggestive rather than causal.

Sources indicate that most studies measured diet and health at a single point in time. Eight drew on the same long-running cohort in Western Australia.

Six research databases were searched by the team, and more than 1,200 articles were screened.

It has been revealed that seventeen studies met the criteria. These studies were published between 2008 and 2019. The children in them ranged from age 1 to age 19.

It has been revealed that studies that scored children’s diets against a set standard of healthy eating were left out. Abebe Abitew’s team kept studies that let the data show how children actually ate.

It has been revealed that in each study, diets were recorded with food questionnaires, 24-hour recalls or food diaries. Statistics were then used to find the foods that tended to be eaten together.

Together, the 17 studies reported 39 eating patterns under many different names. These patterns were sorted into two groups by the reviewers.

Sources indicate that vegetables, fruit, whole grains, legumes and fish formed the core of the healthy patterns. Processed meats, refined grains, fried potatoes, sugary drinks, sweets and takeaway food were typical of the unhealthy ones.

Twenty of the 39 patterns fell in the unhealthy group. Each study then compared children who followed a pattern closely with children who followed it less.

Four of the studies dealt with mental health, and all four involved teenagers between 13 and 19.

The first came from Western Australia and involved teenagers aged 13 to 15. Withdrawn, anxious or depressed behavior was scored higher among those who ate more of the unhealthy pattern. Their scores for aggression and delinquency were higher too.

In a recent development, teenagers from the same state were tracked for three years in a second analysis. An unhealthy pattern at age 14 was followed by more aggressive and delinquent behavior at age 17. This link was reported for girls.

Victoria supplied a survey of about 3,300 teenagers. Depression symptoms were more likely among the boys who ate more of an unhealthy pattern.

The fourth study drew on about 1,800 14-year-olds. A high score on the unhealthy pattern went with about twice the odds of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, or ADHD. For the healthy pattern, no such link with ADHD appeared.

Recent findings suggest that just one of these four studies tracked teenagers over time. Diet and mental health were recorded together in the remaining three. For that reason, those three can’t show which came first.

Three further studies dealt with thinking skills and school results.

In a recent development, about 600 teenagers in Western Australia took part in the first. Their diets were recorded at age 14, and their thinking skills were tested at age 17.

Sources indicate that reactions were slower among those who had eaten more of the unhealthy pattern. The same teenagers also made more errors when a maze learned earlier had to be recalled.

Fewer errors were made by those who had eaten more of the healthy pattern.

According to recent reports, A South Australian study involved 315 children between the ages of 9 and 11. Children who ate more sweets, fried food and soft drinks scored lower in reading and numeracy.

Their spelling, grammar and punctuation scores were lower as well, and writing was the single exception.

Industry observers note that the third study reported lower mathematics and reading scores in Western Australian teenagers. Again, the lower scores belonged to those who ate more of the unhealthy pattern.

Recent findings suggest that A single combined estimate had been planned by the team. That plan was dropped because every study relied on its own tests and its own way of scoring diet. The review therefore offers no single figure for the size of the gaps.

Body weight, body fat and related conditions such as fatty liver disease were covered by nine of the 17 studies.

In a recent development, for most eating patterns, no connection with body fat turned up at all. One national study of children aged 2 to 15 is an example. Neither the healthy pattern nor the unhealthy one was linked with body fat there.

According to recent reports, A national survey of 12- to 16-year-olds produced a result in the other direction. Overweight was somewhat less likely among boys who ate more of a high-fat, low-fiber pattern. Among girls, there was no link.

According to recent reports, south Australian children aged 1 to 4 were the subject of another study. Obesity was tied to just one pattern there, and it was built on grains, fruit, vegetables and red meat.

The results had been different in the team’s earlier review of Australian adults. Eating patterns were consistently linked with heart and metabolic disease in that work.

Differences in method may help explain the mixed results in children, the authors wrote.

Recent findings suggest that studies that found no link with body fat were concentrated among those relying on short records. Only one or two days of eating were captured by such records.

A child’s diet changes from one day to the next, so a real link can be weakened by short records. A different tool was used in most of the Western Australian studies.

That questionnaire listed 212 foods and asked about the previous 12 months.

Sources indicate that eight of the 17 studies drew on the Raine Study. It began in Western Australia between 1989 and 1991 with 2,900 pregnant women. Their 2,868 children have been followed since before birth.

Sources indicate that one group of children is shared by many of the studies. The evidence is therefore narrower than the count of studies suggests.

According to recent reports, the authors wrote that the findings may not apply to all Australian children. First Nations children and those from culturally and linguistically diverse families were among the groups named.

It has been revealed that A whole way of eating is described by a pattern. So the review can’t say which foods within it account for the links.

In a recent development, some outcomes rest on a single study. One study of tooth decay in toddlers found no link with eating patterns. The same was true of one study of brain tumors in children.

Eleven of the 17 studies were rated as high quality by the team, and six as medium. Anxiety disorders, autism, sleep problems and diabetes were not examined in any of the 17.

It has been revealed that only 4.3% of Australian children aged 2 to 17 eat the recommended daily servings of fruit and vegetables. That figure is cited by the authors, and the servings are set by the Australian Dietary Guidelines.

One in three Australian children aged 8 to 13 has a mental health problem. That was found in a poll by the Royal Children’s Hospital in Melbourne.

It has been revealed that the authors pointed to places to act. One is school meal programs, which have been tied to better learning and behavior in earlier research.

Another is the supermarket. About two-thirds of shelf space there goes to foods the guidelines say to limit.

More families have been left short of food by the recent rise in the cost of living, the authors wrote.

“While cost-of-living pressures can make healthy choices challenging, combining nutrition education with structural changes to improve affordability and access to healthy foods is essential for supporting children’s health and development,” Abebe Abitew mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that in none of the 17 studies was a child’s diet changed and the result then measured. So the review can’t say whether improving a child’s diet would improve mental health or grades.

Recent findings suggest that according to the authors, future research should follow children for years. Diets should be recorded repeatedly with the same tools, and changes in diet should be tested directly.

The full study was published in the journal Current Nutrition Reports.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • With the Moon not far from Full, its western limb is now coming into view as the Sun rises across the lunar landscape.
  • In a recent development, zoom in on Schickard to discover that its dark floor isn’t perfectly smooth, but pockmarked by smaller craters that came after the initial, larger crater’s formation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

November 21: Mercury far west of the Sun.

With the Moon not far from Full, its western limb is now coming into view as the Sun rises across the lunar landscape. The large, flat-floored crater Schickard is prominent in the southwest, near the small, circular Mare Humorum. Because the nearly Full Moon is so bright, you may want to use a Moon filter before you turn your telescope toward our satellite tonight for a closer look.

In a recent development, zoom in on Schickard to discover that its dark floor isn’t perfectly smooth, but pockmarked by smaller craters that came after the initial, larger crater’s formation. Its outer walls are shallow and beaten down, also showing off their age. Look closely at Schickard’s western wall to see how it has slumped, particularly compared to the eastern side of the crater rim. Also compare the texture of the southwestern portion of the crater floor, which appears quite rough, to the rest of the crater, which is smoother. The difference arises because most of the crater was flooded by lava, which didn’t quite reach its southwestern regions.

Stretching about 130 miles (210 kilometers) across, Schickard is roughly 4 billion years old and was formed by a giant impact. Because it sits so near the limb of the Moon, it often looks oblong from our vantage point on Earth — but from above, orbiters have shown it is really quite circular in shape.

#145851. Older muscles recover more slowly, and a lingering repair signal may explain why

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1458 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Older muscles recover more slowly, and a lingering repair signal may explain why

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1458 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers found that low-dose ibuprofen improved muscle strength recovery in older mice, but benefits remain untested in humans.
  • It has been revealed that two weeks in bed or in a leg brace can weaken muscles.
  • It has been revealed that part of the reason, according to fresh research, may lie with prostaglandins.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers found that low-dose ibuprofen improved muscle strength recovery in older mice, but benefits remain untested in humans.

It has been revealed that two weeks in bed or in a leg brace can weaken muscles. Older adults can have a harder time regaining that strength.

It has been revealed that part of the reason, according to fresh research, may lie with prostaglandins. These fat-based molecules play a role in healing muscle.

For the study, the hind legs of old mice were kept off the ground for two weeks before recovery began.

Industry observers note that prostaglandin levels in their muscle climbed once recovery began and had not come down a week later. In young mice the levels held fairly steady.

Ibuprofen blocks the production of prostaglandins. Old mice were given a low dose for the first two days of recovery. They ended up with a stronger grip than old mice that received no drug. A higher dose did not help.

A repair signal that lingers too long, the team concluded, may be part of why old muscle bounces back poorly.

According to recent reports, the study was led by Paul-Emile Bourrant while he was a graduate researcher at University of Utah Health. He worked with Micah Drummond, a professor of pathology.

It has been revealed that bourrant remarked the research is aimed at older adults who are recovering from inactivity. Bed rest after hip surgery is one example. If their muscle does not return, these adults can lose their independence.

Recent findings suggest that most of the experiments were carried out in male mice or in cells grown in dishes. The human part involved 11 volunteers, and none of them took ibuprofen.

Muscle loses size and strength quickly when it goes unused after an injury, surgery, or a hospital stay. In aging muscle, that loss is harder to reverse.

In a recent development, to reproduce this disuse, the team kept the hind legs of mice off the ground for 14 days. The animals were then allowed to walk normally for up to a week. The young mice were about 4 months old, and the old mice were about 25 months old.

In a recent development, strength was measured with a grip test. Each mouse held a metal grid with all four paws. A researcher then gently pulled the animal back by the base of its tail. The peak force was recorded by a meter.

In a recent development, both age groups had lost grip strength after 14 days of disuse. After a week of normal walking, the young mice had regained it.

The old mice still had not returned to their starting strength. Muscle mass in the calf was likewise not fully restored.

In a recent development, fat levels in calf muscle were measured by the team at each stage of the experiment. The signaling molecules produced from those fats were measured as well. Six mice from each age group were examined at every stage.

Arachidonic acid is an omega-6 fat stored in cell membranes. During recovery, greater amounts were released from the membranes of old muscle, and the level remained high. In young muscle, it was kept at relatively low levels throughout.

Arachidonic acid serves as the starting material from which prostaglandins are made. That conversion relies on COX enzymes, which happen to be the target of ibuprofen.

It has been revealed that during recovery, several prostaglandins were higher in old mice than in young mice. Young animals revealed little change over the same period.

The authors described that pattern as notable. Signals like these usually fade as muscle repairs itself. Such fading is seen after a session of resistance training, for example.

According to recent reports, drummond said muscle heals with the help of prostaglandins. But when the levels stay high for too long, he said, inflammation can turn chronic. Cells can also become stressed.

The team then turned to people. Five young adults and six healthy older adults took part. Each wore a knee brace on one leg for 14 days. Weight was kept off that leg with crutches or a walker.

The young adults averaged 23 years of age, and the older adults averaged 68. All of them came from the Salt Lake City area and were part of a larger registered trial.

Industry observers note that small samples of thigh muscle were taken from each person at four points. The first was taken before the brace went on, and the second when it came off. Two further samples were collected on days two and seven of recovery.

The human data were less striking than the mouse data. Total levels of the fat-derived signals were not clearly altered during recovery.

After seven days of recovery, two prostaglandins were higher in the older adults than in the young adults. By then, earlier rises in several signals had partly subsided in the younger group.

A slower and smaller response was seen in humans than in mice, the authors wrote. Differences between the two experiments were also noted, including how the muscle was rested and which muscle was sampled.

Sources indicate that aging tissue gradually collects cells that no longer divide but have not died. Such cells are known as senescent cells and are often nicknamed zombie cells. They release inflammatory signals into nearby tissue.

Industry observers note that in old mice, senescent cells in the calf muscle rose by day four of recovery. Their numbers rose further by day seven. A comparable increase was not observed in young muscle.

In the old animals, a greater number of senescent cells was associated with a lower calf muscle mass. A positive association with prostaglandin levels was also observed at day four of recovery.

Senescence was then induced in three types of cultured mouse cells by means of a chemotherapy drug.

No increase in a major prostaglandin was detected in the muscle cells or the connective tissue cells. An increase was detected only in the immune cells known as macrophages.

Cultured muscle fibers were exposed to fluid that had been collected from the senescent macrophages. The fibers were reduced in size as a result. This reduction was partly prevented if a COX enzyme had been blocked in the macrophages.

The question of whether lower prostaglandin levels would improve recovery was then addressed in old mice. After the same 14 days of disuse the animals were injected twice daily during the first two days of walking.

Industry observers note that the mice were divided into three groups of 7 to 12 animals each. Ibuprofen was given at 30 milligrams per kilogram of body weight per day to the first group. The second group received 60 milligrams per kilogram and the third group was injected without any drug.

It has been revealed that grip strength adjusted for body weight was assessed on day seven of recovery. A higher grip strength was recorded in the low-dose group than in the untreated group.

No difference in calf or lower-leg muscle mass was found between these groups. However, more force for its size was produced by the soleus, a small lower-leg muscle, in laboratory tests.

Less collagen, the fibrous material of scar tissue, was seen in stained sections of the calf. Two of the three markers of senescent cells were also reduced.

Industry observers note that these benefits were not observed in the high-dose group. In the paper, the authors suggested that complete COX suppression might disrupt the remodeling of muscle.

Dose and timing may also account for the mixed results of earlier research on these drugs and muscle, they added.

In one trial, older adults who took COX-blocking drugs during resistance training gained more muscle and strength.

“We don’t have the full picture yet,” Bourrant stated.

Industry observers note that ibuprofen was not given to any of the human volunteers. Its effects were tested only in old male mice, at two doses over two days.

The human comparison was small, with 11 people, and female mice were left out. Because muscle ages differently in males and females, testing in females is still needed, the authors wrote.

Recent findings suggest that it also remains unclear which cells produce the extra prostaglandins inside living muscle. In dishes, senescent macrophages made more of one prostaglandin. The authors called for animal experiments to pin down the cells responsible.

For any treatment that targets prostaglandins in aging muscle, the authors wrote, the dose and the timing will matter.

Future studies could test whether a short, low dose during recovery helps older people the way it helped old mice.

The full study was published in the journal Aging Cell.

What happens when gamers swap their chairs for standing desks?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (988 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Standing gave gamers an early boost in a soccer video game, but half ended their standing sessions early because of fatigue or leg discomfort.
  • In a recent development, standing at a desk feels like the healthy choice, the thing you do instead of slumping in a chair all afternoon.
  • According to recent reports, early on, players standing at a desk reported a better mood and took more shots in a soccer video game.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Standing gave gamers an early boost in a soccer video game, but half ended their standing sessions early because of fatigue or leg discomfort.

In a recent development, standing at a desk feels like the healthy choice, the thing you do instead of slumping in a chair all afternoon. Put a gamer at one for three hours and the picture splits into two halves.

According to recent reports, early on, players standing at a desk reported a better mood and took more shots in a soccer video game. At 15 minutes, they also handled distractions better on a test than they had before play.

It has been revealed that by the one-hour mark, players were more fatigued and had more trouble ignoring distractions than when they sat. Five of the ten ended their standing sessions early because of fatigue or leg discomfort.

Takashi Matsui, an associate professor in the Institute of Health and Sport Sciences at the University of Tsukuba in Japan, ran that test and a second one.

In the second, a chair tilted slightly forward gave players some of the same early lift, and none of them quit.

After three hours of reclined play, accuracy on the arrow test hadn’t declined significantly from the start.

Industry observers note that the chairs and desk came from a furniture maker, and so did part of the funding. That’s part of the story, and it’s told below.

Matsui’s team recruited 25 men between 18 and 35 who played video games regularly but never competed.

Ten of them took part in the first experiment and played the soccer game eFootball 2022 for up to three hours on two separate days.

One day they stood at a height-adjustable desk, and the other they sat in a gaming chair, in random order.

Sources indicate that every so often the players stopped for tests, run in the free psychology software PsychoPy. The one that moved was a simple arrows task: pick the direction of a central arrow while ignoring the arrows beside it.

Fifteen minutes into standing play, the players handled that distraction faster than before they started.

Standing players also reported more energy and more pleasure through the first hour. In the game, between 15 and 60 minutes, they took more shots, put more of them on target, and shot more accurately.

Their hearts beat faster the whole time, their pupils were wider, and their saliva carried more cortisol and testosterone for the first half hour.

In a recent development, by the one-hour mark the arrows test had flipped. Standing players were now slower to shake off the distraction than they were seated, and they reported more fatigue.

Five of the ten stopped standing before the three hours were up, on average after about 103 minutes.

Standing sessions ran about 142 minutes on average against the full 180 seated.

Enjoyment was lower at the end of standing play than seated play, and the players who quit standing conceded more goals in their last match than players who finished.

The authors suggested that the effort of standing may have contributed to the later fatigue and difficulty ignoring distractions.

For the second experiment, the team seated 15 different men in the same chair, set two ways: tilted 10 degrees forward, or reclined 23 degrees.

Each man played for three hours in both positions on separate days.

Industry observers note that no one quit either seated session. Leaning forward, players reported more energy through the first two hours and, in the first half hour, took more shots, more shots on target, and more passes than when reclined.

At 60 minutes they also handled the arrows distraction faster.

It has been revealed that then the forward lean ran out. By three hours, those players were less accurate on the arrows test than at the start, while accuracy in the reclined position highlighted no significant decline from the start.

Reclining had its own signature in the game, too, with more interceptions.

Both the desk and the gaming chair were made by Okamura, a Japanese office furniture company.

Okamura helped fund the study through a contract research grant to Matsui, and four of its employees are co-authors.

The researchers noted that the funders had no role in the design, the analysis, or the decision to publish.

Players came from the university and from gaming communities in Tokyo’s Akihabara district.

It has been revealed that each was paid 5,000 yen for about five hours in the lab, which was kept at 73°F (23°C). They drank water in small amounts and skipped caffeine and alcohol beforehand.

Every arrows test was taken sitting in one standard position, whatever posture the player had been gaming in.

Two other distraction tests, one with color words and one with shapes appearing on the wrong side, demonstrated no posture effect at all.

Industry observers note that the authors list the limits plainly. Twenty-five people is a small group for the number of things measured, the study was not registered in advance, and the players were young men playing one soccer game.

Whether any of this holds for women, older players, shooters, or an office job is untested.

The physiology is a sketch, not a mechanism. The team measured heart rate, hormones, blood sugar, and pupils, but not brain or muscle activity, so why standing or leaning helped early and hurt later isn’t settled.

Sources indicate that the practical question is one the team didn’t test. If leaning forward helps early and reclining helps late, switching between them during a long session might capture both.

Whether it does, and how often a player should switch, is unknown, and the authors name self-chosen posture changes during real play as the next thing to measure.

The full study was published in the journal Computers in Human Behavior Reports.

Latest Update: Some fish in Montana live past 130, and their longevity may conceal a problem

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (895 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Blue suckers in Montana’s Upper Missouri River can live to 131, but few young fish appear to be joining the population.
  • According to new research, blue suckers in Montana’s Upper Missouri River can survive for more than 130 years.
  • The study was co-led by Alec Lackmann at the University of Minnesota Duluth.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Blue suckers in Montana’s Upper Missouri River can live to 131, but few young fish appear to be joining the population.

According to new research, blue suckers in Montana’s Upper Missouri River can survive for more than 130 years. Their extraordinary longevity may be concealing trouble: too few young fish are joining the population.

The study was co-led by Alec Lackmann at the University of Minnesota Duluth. Fellow leaders were Luke Holmquist of Montana Fish, Wildlife & Parks and Allen Andrews at the University of Hawai’i at Mānoa.

According to recent reports, the blue sucker, Cycleptus elongatus, is native to 23 states. It is listed under various conservation concern categories in 22.

In Montana, biologists measured 1,056 blue suckers between 1996 and 2024. Almost 96% exceeded 65 centimeters in length, and average body size gradually increased.

Small fish were scarce throughout those decades. The adults were still there, but few younger fish seemed to be replacing them.

“For decades, there has been conservation concern for the species across much of its range,” the researchers wrote.

“Nonetheless, no validated age-based life history information exists for the species, which is a major knowledge gap.”.

The team examined 42 fish collected in 2023 and 2024, including recovered carcasses. Their estimated ages ranged from eight to 131 years.

Sources indicate that earlier studies had reported maximum ages of 42 and, subsequently, 61 years. The newly introduced maximum more than doubles that later estimate.

Sources indicate that the answer lay in earstones, or otoliths, inside the fishes’ skulls. These structures accumulate yearly growth bands, which researchers count under a microscope after cutting thin sections.

“Blue suckers have extremely small otoliths, smaller than the buffalofishes, but we figured out how to work with them,” Lackmann mentioned.

After counting those bands, “we were seeing the population had ages up to 130 years old,” he mentioned.

“When age estimates are that much older than previously thought, an additional line of evidence is needed to rigorously test their validity.”.

That second check came from an unlikely source: nuclear weapons tests. The radioactive carbon they released left a dated signal in material growing at the time.

“Thermonuclear bombs that were tested in the mid to late 1950s and early 1960s more than doubled the amount of radiocarbon in the atmosphere,” Lackmann stated.

Sources indicate that “This left a time-specific marker in organisms that lived through the bomb pulse. And if you’re able to quantify growth bands in an individual (for example, in trees, otoliths of bony fish, etc.) that is estimated to have lived through the bomb pulse, you can actually test to determine if the ages you are quantifying are accurate.”.

“Bomb radiocarbon dating is one of the best ways to age-validate long-lived organisms. So that’s where we have multiple lines of evidence here, otoliths providing the age estimates, and bomb radiocarbon confirming and validating the otolith ages and extreme longevity of the blue sucker.“.

Industry observers note that the team checked samples within individual earstones and across different fish. The radiocarbon rise and peak matched the timing predicted from the growth bands.

It has been revealed that half the sampled fish were at least 99 years old. About 64% had hatched before Fort Peck Dam was completed in 1940.

Successful recruitment, meaning young fish surviving to join the population, became less likely after major dams were built.

Evidence of recruitment was stronger in years with higher spring flows. Even at comparable flows, recruitment was less likely after 1954.

Sources indicate that dams can change currents, block migration routes, and alter nursery habitats. The researchers have yet to establish which mechanisms are restricting young blue suckers’ survival.

Old age alone did not appear to prevent reproduction. Tissue examinations found males and females capable of spawning across ages ranging from 19 to 130 years.

That leaves an urgent question: what happens between spawning and the arrival of a new generation?

Such longevity is especially surprising in a species whose adults live year-round in fast-flowing rivers.

Those habitats demand energy, and researchers generally associate them with a faster pace of life.

Blue suckers now join bigmouth buffalo, smallmouth buffalo, and black buffalo as four sucker species known to reach 100. All four discoveries have come since 2019.

Sources indicate that their long lives can carry populations through years of poor breeding conditions. But surviving adults can also make prolonged recruitment problems harder to recognize.

The findings come from a single population near the northern edge of the species’ range. Lifespans in other populations will need their own investigation.

The authors call for research into reconnecting spawning and nursery habitats, and restoring river conditions that help young fish survive.

For Holmquist, the ages also make the transformation of the river unusually tangible.

“To put a timeline on some of those older fish: the oldest one hatched around two years after Montana became a state, around the dawn of the automobile, like 20 years before the Titanic sank – it’s just wild,” Holmquist said.

“We start putting it in the context of what the landscape looked like when these fish hatched, and all the changes that have happened since – and they just keep swimming along in the river.”.

The study is published in the journal Communications Biology.

A stunning stellar nursery lurks at the northern border of Corona Australis. The Corona Australis Molecular Cloud fills the left side of this image with glowing gas and dark dust. Although most of the newly forming stars remain hidden within this web, the variable R Coronae Australis just shines through. It dwells in the orange cloud to the lower left of the bright emission nebula that dominates just left of center. Several bluish reflection nebulae also populate this area. The molecular cloud lies 430 light-years away, among the closest star-forming regions to Earth, and holds enough material to create thousands of stars. Contrast that with the Chandelier Cluster (NGC 6723) at upper right. This globular contains hundreds of thousands of stars and resides about 28,000 light-years from us. It inhabits far southern Sagittarius.

Richard Talcott is a former senior editor and current contributing editor of Astronomy.

#145847. What does space radiation do to the brain’s immune cells?

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

What does space radiation do to the brain’s immune cells?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (850 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Simulated space radiation altered gene activity in the brain’s immune cells, with different effects in male and female mice.
  • Earth’s atmosphere and magnetic field shield people on the ground from much of the radiation that astronauts encounter on missions to the Moon or Mars.
  • Industry observers note that galactic cosmic rays are highly energetic particles found in space.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Simulated space radiation altered gene activity in the brain’s immune cells, with different effects in male and female mice.

Earth’s atmosphere and magnetic field shield people on the ground from much of the radiation that astronauts encounter on missions to the Moon or Mars.

Industry observers note that galactic cosmic rays are highly energetic particles found in space. According to NOAA, they carry enough energy to damage spacecraft electronics.

NASA wants to know what they do to human brains.

Industry observers note that A University of Rochester lab has spent more than 15 years on this question. Professor of Neuroscience M. Kerry O’Banion, MD, PhD, has led the work.

In earlier research, his team found that simulated space radiation accelerated Alzheimer’s-related changes in mice.

“We know cognitive changes from exposure to radiation in space are a real risk,” O’Banion noted.

Industry observers note that “It’s key we understand how brain cells are changed. Knowing which mechanisms are impacted and how may help the development of countermeasures to protect or lessen an astronaut’s exposure to space radiation.”.

In mice, simulated space radiation altered gene activity in the brain’s immune cells differently in males and females.

It has been revealed that the researchers detected no short-term behavioral or cognitive changes in either sex. The team is still looking at the long-term effects.

“Additional studies examining other time points and effects in other experimental systems will be required to understand this further,” O’Banion remarked.

According to recent reports, the experiments ran at the NASA Space Radiation Laboratory at Brookhaven National Laboratory on Long Island. Researchers used simulated space radiation, produced by particle accelerators.

According to recent reports, at the time, Brookhaven was the only facility in the world with that technology. There are now two.

Neuroscience graduate student Mark Osabutey led the project. He used single-cell RNA sequencing to examine nearly 16,000 microglia.

These are the brain’s immune cells. They came from male and female mice exposed to simulated galactic cosmic radiation.

“Surprisingly, despite clear molecular changes, we found no widespread inflammatory activation or measurable radiation-associated behavioral impairment at the time we examined,” Osabutey mentioned.

According to recent reports, he suggested the molecular responses may happen earlier. Or they may not be tied to detectable functional impairment at all.

Male and female microglia showed distinct responses.

In the male brain, changes were linked to cellular stress adaptation and metabolism. In the female brain, microglia showed broader reductions in immune signaling pathways.

It’s unclear whether these changes are protective, harmful, or temporary.

Recent findings suggest that researchers did find one shared change. Both sexes had more of a protein called FKBP5 in two brain regions, the cortex and the dentate gyrus. FKBP5 helps regulate how cells respond to stress.

“We now need to understand whether FKBP5 plays a protective or harmful role, and how different radiation exposures and other spaceflight stressors influence long-term brain health,” Osabutey explained.

“Our findings highlight the importance of considering biological sex when assessing neurological risks during spaceflight and identify potential pathways for developing protective strategies.”.

Osabutey has worked on NASA-funded research since joining the O’Banion lab.

Sources indicate that in 2023, he received a predoctoral grant augmentation award from NASA. This grant funded his study of population-level changes in microglia after galactic cosmic radiation exposure.

“Receiving NASA support has allowed me to contribute to research addressing questions of national and international importance,” Osabutey said.

“As a physician-scientist in training, I could not have asked for a better environment in which to train, and the experience has taught me how to pursue meaningful scientific questions through rigorous basic/translational investigation and collaboration, skills that I will carry forward in my future efforts to better understand brain injury and neurological disease.”.

“Graduate students and postdoctoral fellows have been an essential part of our NASA research effort,” O’Banion added.

“It’s comprised of a large team that includes the outstanding organizational skills of our long-time senior research technician, Lee Trojanczyk, as well as support personnel at Brookhaven National Labs. Over time, nearly a dozen University of Rochester trainees have contributed to this work.”.

It has been revealed that long trips to deep space are not just an engineering problem. They are a biology problem.

This study adds an notable detail: the same dose of radiation may not land the same way in every brain.

Industry observers note that male and female brains showed different molecular responses. That doesn’t settle whether one sex is more vulnerable.

It does suggest that future risk assessments should account for sex. It also points to a specific protein, FKBP5, worth watching.

The researchers detected no behavioral or cognitive impairment in the mice at the time they tested them. That leaves open whether effects emerge later.

It has been revealed that for now, the finding is a step in understanding how space travel changes the brain. It won’t keep astronauts home, but it may help keep them safe when they go.

The study is published in the journal Scientific Reports.
