Latest Update: How air pollution contributes to lung cancer even in people who have never smoked

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (907 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A newly introduced review explores how fine particles in polluted air may fuel lung cancer by creating conditions that help cells with existing mutations grow.
  • Tiny airborne particles can encourage lung cancer by changing the conditions around cells that already carry harmful mutations.
  • A newly introduced review explains how inflammation helps this happen, including in people who have never smoked.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A newly introduced review explores how fine particles in polluted air may fuel lung cancer by creating conditions that help cells with existing mutations grow.

Tiny airborne particles can encourage lung cancer by changing the conditions around cells that already carry harmful mutations.

A newly introduced review explains how inflammation helps this happen, including in people who have never smoked.

Industry observers note that the study was led by Kezhong Chen at Peking University People’s Hospital. The international team organizes existing evidence into 12 features spanning cancer’s beginnings, growth, and spread.

It has been revealed that the link with air pollution is well established. The International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies outdoor air pollution and its particulate component as carcinogenic to humans.

Much of the review focuses on PM2.5, particles measuring 2.5 micrometers or less across. Their size allows them to reach deep into the lungs.

Several cohort studies linked each additional 10 micrograms of PM2.5 per cubic meter to a 7–16% higher lung cancer rate. These estimates describe associations across populations, rather than an individual’s chance of developing cancer.

Pollution also varies in composition. Particles from traffic, coal burning, and other sources carry different mixtures of metals and organic chemicals.

Industry observers note that cancer-driving mutations can exist in apparently healthy lung tissue without immediately producing a tumor. What happens around those cells may help determine whether they become dangerous.

It has been revealed that in mouse experiments discussed in the review, PM2.5 drew immune cells called macrophages into the lungs. These cells released interleukin-1 beta, an inflammatory signal.

That environment changed the behavior of alveolar type 2 cells, which help maintain the lung’s air sacs. Cells carrying an EGFR mutation acquired a more immature, progenitor-like state that enabled tumor formation.

This gives pollution a role beyond causing fresh DNA damage. It can also encourage the expansion of cells that already carry mutations.

Industry observers note that the same particles can also damage DNA and interfere with its repair. Both routes may contribute, depending on exposure and the cells involved.

The authors arrange their 12 features across three stages: initiation, progression, and metastasis.

Early changes include vulnerable lung cells, DNA damage, and altered control of gene activity. Persistent inflammation helps create conditions in which abnormal cells can survive.

As tumors develop, the framework describes changes in metabolism, blood-vessel growth, and immune defenses. These changes can help cancer cells obtain resources and escape attack.

Later mechanisms may help tumor cells move through tissue and enter the circulation.

Experimental evidence also suggests pollution can alter distant organs, potentially making them more welcoming to spreading cancer.

According to recent reports, the strength of evidence differs between these mechanisms. Many links still need to be tested directly in human lung tissue.

The review describes clinical patterns that deserve closer investigation, particularly among never-smokers in East Asia.

In one Taiwanese screening study, more than 80% of positive findings involved ground-glass or partly solid nodules. These appear hazy on scans, rather than entirely solid.

It has been revealed that nearly 18% of affected patients had multiple primary lung cancers. That means separate tumors arose independently, rather than one cancer simply spreading.

Molecular studies also point to more frequent EGFR mutations and fewer mutations overall than in smokers’ tumors. Some show changes associated with APOBEC enzymes and lack the familiar tobacco-related signature called SBS4.

None of these features can, by itself, identify pollution as the cause of someone’s cancer.

It has been revealed that exposure alone does not explain everyone’s vulnerability. Older adults generally demonstrated stronger associations between particulate pollution and lung cancer.

Sources indicate that the review also describes evidence that inherited susceptibility matters. UK Biobank findings linked higher genetic risk and greater pollution exposure with increased vulnerability.

Yet the research map poorly matches the pollution map. South Asia, Southeast Asia, and Africa carry substantial burdens, while much of the evidence comes from Europe and North America.

Differences in fuels, housing, workplaces, and access to care make it difficult to assume findings transfer unchanged between regions.

Recent findings suggest that the review gathers evidence from earlier studies; it does not validate a newly introduced diagnostic test. No established PM-specific biomarker can yet identify affected patients.

Human studies must disentangle pollution from occupation, indoor smoke, and socioeconomic circumstances. Those exposures often overlap.

In a recent development, laboratory conditions present another problem. Some animal studies place unusually large doses directly into the airways, while short experiments poorly represent years of exposure.

Recent findings suggest that flat cell cultures also miss the lung’s architecture and interactions between different cell types. The authors want more realistic exposure models, longer follow-up and detailed analysis of human tissue.

The team also wants better records of personal exposure, using tools such as wearable sensors alongside neighborhood pollution measurements.

Many screening programs prioritize smoking history. In the United States, Preventive Services Task Force recommendations target certain adults with substantial smoking histories.

The authors argue that pollution exposure should help inform future risk models, alongside age and other factors.

Establishing who benefits from screening will still require evidence that balances earlier detection against unnecessary investigations.

“We wanted to trace the multiple layers of that pathway and to give early screening and intervention for high-risk groups a scientific basis,” the authors concluded.

The study is published in the journal The Innovation.

America’s fastest ocean liner was purposely sunk off the Florida coast, making it the world’s largest artificial reef

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The SS United States, once the fastest transatlantic ocean liner, was sunk off Florida in November 2026 to become the world's largest artificial reef.
  • The SS United States, a 990-foot (302-meter) ocean liner, was sent to the bottom of the Gulf on November 11, 2026.
  • Okaloosa County, Florida, had scheduled the sinking for November 12, about 22 nautical miles (41 kilometers) southwest of Destin-Fort Walton Beach.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The SS United States, once the fastest transatlantic ocean liner, was sunk off Florida in November 2026 to become the world's largest artificial reef.

The SS United States, a 990-foot (302-meter) ocean liner, was sent to the bottom of the Gulf on November 11, 2026.

Okaloosa County, Florida, had scheduled the sinking for November 12, about 22 nautical miles (41 kilometers) southwest of Destin-Fort Walton Beach. It bills the wreck as the world’s largest artificial reef.

In a recent development, the county’s initiative put the ship in about 180 feet (55 meters) of water. Her upper deck would sit about 55 feet (17 meters) below the surface.

Her keel was laid on February 8, 1950, at the Newport News Shipbuilding and Dry Dock Organization in Virginia. Designed by naval architect William Francis Gibbs, she was the largest passenger ship ever built in the United States.

She left Latest York on her first crossing in July 1952, bound for Le Havre and Southampton. She covered the 2,949 nautical miles (5,465 kilometers) from the Ambrose light vessel to Bishop Rock lighthouse in 3 days, 10 hours and 40 minutes.

Recent findings suggest that her average speed topped 35 knots (40 mph, or 65 kilometers per hour), according to Guinness World Records. In trials the month before, she had reached 38.32 knots (44 mph, or 71 kilometers per hour).

Recent findings suggest that on that voyage, she broke the transatlantic speed record in both directions. She was also the first American ship in 100 years to win the Blue Riband, says the SS United States Conservancy.

Built to be converted into a troop transport in the event of war, she could carry 14,000 troops 10,000 miles (16,000 kilometers) without refueling.

The liner was withdrawn from service in 1969. In 1996, she was towed to Philadelphia, where she stayed docked on the Delaware River for nearly three decades.

According to recent reports, A rent dispute over the ship’s Philadelphia pier ended up in federal court. The Conservancy, which bought the ship in 2011, had been paying $850 a day under a berthing agreement.

It has been revealed that A June 14, 2024, ruling rejected the pier owner’s demand to double the rent to $1,700 a day. It also required the Conservancy to remove the ship by September 12.

“The judge’s decision gives us a very limited window to find a upcoming home for the SS United States and raise the resources necessary to move the ship and keep her safe,” Conservancy President Susan Gibbs stated after the ruling.

That October, Okaloosa County signed a purchase and sale agreement with the Conservancy, estimating up to $10.1 million for acquisition, remediation, transport and deployment. The county later allocated $13 million to the entire project, paid for with tourist bed taxes and contributions from partners.

According to recent reports, after a 1,800-nautical-mile (3,300-kilometer) tow, the ship reached Mobile, Alabama, in March 2025 to be prepared for sinking. Both funnels, the radar mast and a propeller were removed and stored for a planned land-based museum, and more than 400 portholes were kept.

“This will be a historic day for Destin-Fort Walton Beach and for a ship with such a historic story,” Trey Goodwin, chairman of the Okaloosa County Board of County Commissioners, remarked in October.

Before a ship becomes a reef, fuel, oil, asbestos and polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) are among the materials of concern, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency notes. Properly prepared, a vessel is meant to be environmentally sound as a reef, unlike wrecks leaking explosives.

Recent findings suggest that all 128 fuel and lubricant tanks on the SS United States were emptied, cleaned and certified clean by a marine chemist. Crews collected more than 200 samples to check for PCBs.

Industry observers note that all of the green exterior floor covering, which held high concentrations of PCBs, was removed. Work on all 12 decks also removed ventilation systems, flaking paint and wiring, with no negative findings in final inspections, the county’s tourism department reported.

Plans also called for cutting back the aluminum superstructure to allow a shallower placement. Holes were to be cut so the ship would land upright, and passages opened for marine life.

Industry observers note that the project received a 10-year federal re-authorization permit. A December 2025 county presentation also ruled out the use of explosives.

The aircraft carrier USS Oriskany was sunk off Pensacola on May 17, 2006. The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission lists her as 911 feet (278 meters) long, at a depth of 212 feet (65 meters).

The SS United States is longer, but Guinness World Records still lists the Oriskany as the largest artificial reef.

Sources indicate that officials expect the wreck to draw grouper, snapper, mackerel, tuna and wahoo. Her top deck is meant to be within reach of all levels of certified divers.

Researchers from three institutions have partnered with the project to study the new reef. One will run 10 years of biological, chemical and physical monitoring, and the others will study its reef soundscape and tagged fish.

The ship joins more than a dozen large vessels already sunk in the Gulf by the county’s Natural Resources Team.

The information was obtained from Okaloosa County.

It has been revealed that born Nov. 22, 1942, in Philadelphia, Guion “Guy” Bluford went on to major in aerospace engineering at Penn State. In addition to training as a fighter pilot in the Air Force, Bluford also earned master’s and doctoral degrees from the Air Force Institute of Technology. In 1978, he was selected to be a space shuttle astronaut in Astronaut Group 8 — one of just 35 people chosen from 10,000 applicants.

In a recent development, bluford introduced as a mission specialist on Challenger for STS-8 on Aug. 30, 1983, becoming the first African American in space. Three additional space shuttle missions would follow, bringing Bluford’s total time in space up to 688 hours – including NASA’s first night launch and night landing of the space shuttle and the largest crew in space (eight people on one spaceflight). In 1993, he retired from the military and NASA; today he continues to work in the private sector of the aerospace industry.

#145841. What do cadaver dogs smell when they find a buried body?

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (965 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

What do cadaver dogs smell when they find a buried body?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (965 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a pilot study, three cadaver dogs and an electronic nose searched the same grave to see how the dogs’ alerts lined up with the device’s readings.
  • According to recent reports, when a cadaver dog lies down over a patch of ground, a search team treats it as the word of an expert.
  • Handlers train the dogs on bone and fluid from decomposing bodies, but the exact chemicals a dog responds to are still unknown.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a pilot study, three cadaver dogs and an electronic nose searched the same grave to see how the dogs’ alerts lined up with the device’s readings.

According to recent reports, when a cadaver dog lies down over a patch of ground, a search team treats it as the word of an expert. The expert can’t explain its reasoning, though.

Handlers train the dogs on bone and fluid from decomposing bodies, but the exact chemicals a dog responds to are still unknown.

Over two months, an Australian research team tested three police dogs and a handheld electronic nose at the same grave.

The dogs located the grave consistently after researchers probed the soil, and the electronic nose picked up stronger signals after probing.

The study rests on a single buried donor and three dogs, so the authors call it a pilot.

Amber Brown, now at the University of North Florida, conducted the research while completing her doctorate at the University of Technology Sydney.

Maiken Ueland, who directs the forensic research site where the body was buried, supervised it, with co-authors at the University of Windsor in Canada and in China.

“We don’t know exactly what they are smelling – whether it’s a single compound or a combination of compounds,” Ueland remarked.

“The electronic nose can provide greater certainty during training by showing whether decomposition odor is present in an area, including when a dog does not alert.”.

The body belonged to a 79-year-old man who donated it to research. Five days after his death in March 2020, staff buried him about 2 feet (60 centimeters) down in a 12-acre (4.9-hectare) forest plot in western Sydney.

Three empty graves were dug the same day so the dogs couldn’t simply react to disturbed soil.

The grave then sat untouched for 98 days, long enough to match the standard definition of a long-term missing person. Searches ran on six days between July and September.

That is a Sydney winter, with daily averages between 48°F and 57°F (9°C and 14°C), when buried bodies give off less odor.

Sources indicate that on five of the six search days, the team pushed a probe into the grave at 14 points to let trapped gas escape. Soil holds the chemicals of decay the way a sponge holds water, and a probe hole opens a path out.

The dogs came from the Upcoming South Wales Police Force canine unit. Two were English springer spaniels, aged three and seven and a half, and one was a four-year-old Labrador retriever.

The youngest had about a year of experience and the oldest about six.

None had worked a buried body before. Each dog was released off leash about 500 feet (150 meters) from the grave, from a different direction each visit, and alerted by lying down or barking.

The handlers didn’t know where the grave was on the first visit, but the head trainer did, and watched from a distance to rule on each alert.

The electronic nose, called NOS.E, carries five gas sensors tuned to the chemical families that buried bodies release, such as alcohols and compounds containing nitrogen or sulfur.

Recent findings suggest that before each dog ran, a researcher walked it over the grave with its intake about 6 inches (15 centimeters) above the ground. An empty control grave 16 feet (5 meters) away was sampled the same way.

After probing, every dog tested alerted over the donor’s upper torso, where the device registered its strongest readings.

Over the whole trial, the sensors for nitrogen and sulfur compounds and for alcohols responded most.

Sources indicate that the two younger dogs each gave a false alert during searches before probing. The oldest dog never gave a false alert.

Once the grave was probed, no dog missed it and none alerted in the wrong place.

In a recent development, air samples sent to a lab confirmed the same chemical families were present on every search day. They surged after heavy rain and a warm spell around days 126 and 147.

With so few alerts to compare, the statistics could not confirm a link between sensor strength and correct alerts, though correct alerts tended to come with higher readings.

Brown said the device could give trainers another way to check whether a dog’s alert coincides with a chemical signal consistent with decomposition.

“For younger dogs in particular, the technology could help trainers determine whether a dog is genuinely responding to decomposition odor or being influenced by another cue,” she noted.

The device is not meant to replace the dogs. A dog covers ground rapidly and smells things no sensor array can, while the device uses sensors that respond to broad groups of chemicals.

On the last day the probe punctured the remains, and every sensor fired at once on gases a normal search would never release.

One donor, buried at one depth in one season, is the whole dataset.

The dogs may have learned where the grave was over six visits, even though they started from different spots each time.

And the device has not been tested against other soils, deeper burials, or mixed smells, so it is not ready for a real search.

Whether a dog alerts to a single compound, a mix, or a concentration is still the open question.

Sources indicate that ueland’s team intends a larger study with several donors and more dogs over repeated visits. The hard part, she noted, will be keeping the dogs and handlers from learning the sites.

Until that study runs, the pairing has been tried on one grave, and there the sensors and the dogs agreed.

The full study was published in the journal PLOS One.

Independents decide the election, again!

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1181 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A group of fresh senators-elect gather for a photo in Minority Leader Charles E.
  • Once more, independents were the decisive factor in what amounts to the Republicans’ midterm disaster that was both broad and deep.
  • “We hired you to fix the Biden economy and you failed.” Pretty simple.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A group of fresh senators-elect gather for a photo in Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer’s office in Washington on Monday. The large class of incoming Democratic senators was propelled by votes from independents, Winston writes. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

Once more, independents were the decisive factor in what amounts to the Republicans’ midterm disaster that was both broad and deep. No one who reads this column should have been surprised that this growing segment of the electorate became the equivalent of the “deciders-in-chief” who used their vote to send a tough message to the president and his party.

“We hired you to fix the Biden economy and you failed.” Pretty simple.

It has been revealed that according to the exit polls, Democrats won independents by an astonishing 22 points. If this holds, it will be the largest margin in the history of exit polling, beating the Republican margin in 2010 of 19 points. For Republicans, this is the fifth consecutive election losing independents.

It was the size of the GOP defeat with independents that put the number of states and congressional districts into play, districts that President Donald Trump won in 2024, many by double digits.

Independents made up 33 percent of the electorate; Democrats were at 35 percent and Republicans at 32 percent. This is the second consecutive election where independents were a larger part of the electorate than one of the major parties. It also shows that while independents may not have been enthused about voting, they revealed up.

Looking at the 13 battleground Senate races, which now include Mississippi, Democrats won independents in all of them by double digits, and 10 of them by 20 points or more. The independent vote allowed Democrats to overwhelm significant Republican Party ID advantages in many red states and districts.

For example, in Kansas (exit poll not final), Republicans had a 17-point party advantage, but lost independents by 33. Incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall went down with a 5-point loss. In South Carolina, Republicans had a 14-point party advantage, but lost independents by 31 points. A liberal activist Democrat beat a neophyte Republican candidate, appointed Sen. Darline Graham, by 4 points.

In a recent development, despite Texas Republicans’ 5-point party ID advantage, Ken Paxton lost independents by 31 points and lost the Senate race by a huge 12 points. It goes without saying that voters in Texas shocked Republicans by not only rejecting the president’s primary choice for Senate, but taking down all Republicans in statewide races.

It has been revealed that overall, Republicans lost six states with key Senate races where Trump won by double digits in 2024, with Mississippi being a potential seventh. In the House (with 7 races yet to be called at the time of this writing), Democrats have won 56 congressional districts that Trump carried in 2024, along with carrying all 201 districts that Harris won.

According to recent reports, clearly, Republican operatives, consultants and the media missed the boat when it came to evaluating the viability of House races. Using the 2024 Trump-Harris race results to assess the safety or vulnerability of a particular seat proved to be the wrong context.

In the spring, I was beginning to see some danger signals in our polling and in public surveys that raised questions for me about just how many House seats were actually in play, fearing perhaps far more than anyone was predicting. By early summer, I decided to undertake a different analysis on the state of current races using the 2020 Trump-Biden results by congressional district. The research found a much larger number of GOP seats could be vulnerable. In the end, the analysis proved to be right. Democrats won all of the 220 districts that Biden carried, and at least 37 seats that Trump won.

According to the exit polls, the independent vote, not surprisingly, was largely driven by the economy, their top glitch concern. Much to the detriment of Trump and the Republicans, 80 percent of independents thought the economy was not good/poor, versus 20 percent who thought the economy was excellent/good. In terms of inflation, 82 percent said it had been a severe or moderate hardship for them, and 89 percent said the cost of living was a crucial or major factor in how they voted for Congress.

Recent findings suggest that the president and his party got the blame. Looking at specific policies, 71 percent of independents thought that Trump’s tariff policies had hurt the national economy, and more broadly, 72 percent remarked his policies had worsened economic conditions in the country. As a result, Trump’s overall job approval among these voters was 29 percent approve with 71 disapproving; 59 percent strongly disapproving. These extraordinarily bad numbers topped even Biden’s worst job approval numbers.

Trump’s decision to ask voters to “pretend I’m on the ballot,” was, in retrospect, a strategic miscalculation. It was a mistake to tell voters that the economy was in great shape when it was clear the majority of people were very unhappy when it came to inflation — the rising cost of gas and groceries.

A little empathy on economic challenges and a lot better explanation of why the Iran conflict was crucial to national security and worth the economic sacrifice would have gone a long way to minimizing the size of the GOP defeat.

Neither happened, and Republicans were overwhelmed by a blue tsunami almost nobody saw coming. Still, despite the size of the Democrats’ win, they would be wrong to see this as an ideological mandate of any sort. The exit polls demonstrated that the electorate remains center-right. Moderates are the largest component at 41 percent, but conservatives still outnumber liberals by a 33-26 margin.

In a recent development, independents have a negative view of both parties. Their view of Republicans is 32 percent favorable and 68 percent unfavorable. However, Democrats are not far behind, at 42 percent favorable and 58 percent unfavorable.

At a policy level when independents were asked which party was better able to handle the economy, 41 percent said the Democratic Party, 28 percent said the Republican Party, and 30 percent said neither. Both parties are well short of a majority. This reflects the fact that the electorate still negatively remembers the Biden economy, but also believes that Republicans didn’t fix it as they promised two years ago.

According to recent reports, democrats would be wise to moderate and not continue down the increasingly extreme progressive path. Republicans and the president need to take a hard look at their own failings and understand that when it comes to voters, especially independents, all the money in the world is no substitute for good candidates with real solutions.

Industry observers note that david Winston is the president of The Winston Group and a longtime adviser to congressional Republicans. He previously served as the director of planning for Speaker Newt Gingrich. He advises Fortune 100 companies, foundations and nonprofit organizations on strategic planning and public policy challenges, as well as serving as an election analyst for CBS News.

#145838. Latest Update: An armored amphibian hunted like a shark 237 million years ago

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1140 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: An armored amphibian hunted like a shark 237 million years ago

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1140 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Two fossils from southern China reveal an armored amphibian that lived entirely at sea 237 million years ago.
  • According to recent reports, no living amphibian is known to spend its entire life in the open ocean.
  • Yet in the Late Triassic, a flat, armored amphibian about 2½ feet (75 centimeters) long lived on the sea floor at least 19 miles (30 kilometers) from the nearest land.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two fossils from southern China reveal an armored amphibian that lived entirely at sea 237 million years ago.

According to recent reports, no living amphibian is known to spend its entire life in the open ocean. For most, seawater draws moisture out through their permeable skin.

Yet in the Late Triassic, a flat, armored amphibian about 2½ feet (75 centimeters) long lived on the sea floor at least 19 miles (30 kilometers) from the nearest land.

Two nearly complete skeletons from southern China provide the first evidence of an amphibian that lived entirely at sea.

The researchers named the species Gerrothorax maritimus. The name maritimus means “of the sea.”.

Their case rests on where the bones lay and what they are made of, plus a suit of armor the animal’s freshwater ancestors already wore.

The fossils were studied by Lipin Diao of the Geological Museum of Guizhou, Ryosuke Motani of the University of California, Davis, and Da-yong Jiang of Peking University, with two colleagues.

“If you think about today’s amphibians, this animal is unusual because it’s big,” Motani said.

“It’s probably, body mass-wise, about the same as the giant salamander, but what’s different is that giant salamanders are elongated whereas this animal is really chunky.”.

Local fossil collectors dug the skeletons out of a quarry in Guanling County, Guizhou Province, in 2004.

Industry observers note that the bones went to the Geological Museum of Guizhou in 2022, when it opened as the province’s official fossil repository. The rock around them is about 237 million years old.

Sources indicate that the same bed has produced large ocean-going ichthyosaurs, animals of the open sea. In the Late Triassic, this rock was the floor of a gulf about 125 miles (200 kilometers) from any large landmass.

The bones argue against a carcass that drifted out from a river. The larger skeleton still has its fingers in place, and fingers are among the first parts a dead four-legged animal loses at sea.

“Carcasses at sea, unless they sink to the bottom right away, tend to dry out and lose limbs prior to sinking to the bottom,” said Motani, a professor in the UC Davis Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences.

“But these animals had their fingers preserved, so that means they probably died near where they lived.”.

Industry observers note that strontium is a metal that animals take in with their water and build into bone. The mix of its forms differs between the open ocean and water that drains off land.

The team measured that mix in dense bone from both skeletons and in the rock around them.

Recent findings suggest that the bone values were close to the global seawater value of the time. The surrounding rock read higher, closer to the older rocks of the nearby land.

The two skeletons also agreed with each other far more closely than the rock samples did, which the authors read as a living body controlling its own chemistry.

In an interview with Earth.com, Motani said the strontium result needed little interpretation.

“I was surprised to see a clean result, which did not require a lot of interpretations to say A or B,” he noted.

Amphibians breathe and drink through their skin, and that’s what fails them in the ocean, Motani said.

A few living species can tolerate brackish water, and some can even withstand brief exposure to seawater.

“This wonderful device, however, does not do its job in sea water and instead works against the animal,” Motani told Earth.com.

Gerrothorax had a way around that long before it reached the sea. Its back was covered in a pavement of bony plates about an inch across and less than a fifth of an inch thick.

Industry observers note that A second layer of bony rods and small plates protected the belly. The lineage also kept internal gills into adulthood, which most living amphibians lose.

The researchers propose that the armor limited water exchange through the skin. If so, the animal may have taken in water by drinking seawater and shed excess salt through its gills, much as marine fish do.

The armor evolved in fresh water as protection from predators, Motani said, and happened to be the right equipment for a later move into the sea.

“There was a freshwater amphibian that happened to have the equipment needed to colonize the sea – the body armor,” he noted.

In a recent development, the larger skeleton is 29 inches (74 centimeters) long as preserved. The skull is only about 5 inches (13 centimeters) long but close to 10 inches (25 centimeters) wide. The armored back reaches about 11 inches (29 centimeters) across.

According to recent reports, the animal’s hind legs are longer than its front legs. The authors read that as a sign it breathed with gills rather than lungs, since lung-breathing sea animals usually need longer front legs to stay balanced in the water.

Industry observers note that the throat bones are heavily built, as strong as those of sharks that feed by suction. So the team pictures a flat animal resting on the bottom, like a wobbegong carpet shark, and swallowing whatever swam too close.

“They would probably just wait at the bottom and then when prey comes around, they would just suck it in,” Motani noted.

The salt-handling system and the feeding style are inferences from bone, since no soft tissue survived.

According to recent reports, nobody knows whether these ancient amphibians had permeable skin like a frog’s. Nor do the fossils say whether Gerrothorax maritimus laid eggs or gave birth to live young, and amphibian eggs do poorly in salt water.

The species also lived in a greenhouse world, much warmer than today’s.

Even a return to those temperatures would probably not open the sea to modern amphibians, the authors wrote, because most of them lose their gills as adults.

Land vertebrates have colonized the ocean roughly 70 times, and this is the only amphibian lineage known to have gone all the way.

Asked by Earth.com where more marine amphibians might turn up, Motani pointed to Triassic marine shales laid down in the tropics of the time.

Industry observers note that the best bet, he said, is near where the ancient Panthalassa and Tethys oceans met. Those rocks are where this one came from, and where China’s Triassic marine reptiles keep appearing.

Whether Gerrothorax maritimus was alone in the sea, or the first of several armored relatives to make the crossing, is the question those shales will have to answer.

Until a second one turns up, the whole case for a marine amphibian rests on two skeletons from one quarry.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Ecology & Evolution.

Clément Daniel from Pleine-Fougères, France.

The Small Magellanic Cloud (NGC 292), a dwarf satellite galaxy of the Milky Way about 200,000 light-years away, appears to the naked eye like a fuzzy white patch, comprising billions of stars. But narrowband filters reveal it is also studded with glowing clouds of hydrogen, oxygen, and sulfur gas, many of them stellar nurseries.

Hacienda des étoiles, Chile · 6-inch TS-Optics Hypergraph 150 astrograph at f/2.8 · ZWO ASI2600MM Pro camera · 56.9 hours of total exposure (Hα 17.2 hours, OIII 14.3 hours, SII 18.7 hours, LRGB 2, 1.5, 1.5 and 1.8 hours).

#145836. Mangrove forests are using washed up ocean weeds to build their soil and fight rising sea levels

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1279 w)

Mangrove forests are using washed up ocean weeds to build their soil and fight rising sea levels

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1279 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Coastal mangrove forests are critical for protecting shorelines from severe storms and trapping CO2.
  • In a recent development, mangrove forests grow right at the edge of the sea, so rising water can drown them.
  • Before sunrise on his monthly survey days, from May 2022 to May 2024, Florida International University (FIU) doctoral student Kevin Montenegro loaded a 16-foot (4.9-meter) canoe onto a truck and set off to paddle for an hour to the Biscayne Bay mangroves.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Coastal mangrove forests are critical for protecting shorelines from severe storms and trapping CO2. Unfortunately, they are losing the race against rising sea levels.

In a recent development, mangrove forests grow right at the edge of the sea, so rising water can drown them. To survive, the ground under the trees has to build up as fast as the ocean rises. A upcoming study finds that dead seagrass helps that happen.

Before sunrise on his monthly survey days, from May 2022 to May 2024, Florida International University (FIU) doctoral student Kevin Montenegro loaded a 16-foot (4.9-meter) canoe onto a truck and set off to paddle for an hour to the Biscayne Bay mangroves.

He then waded in to see what the tide had left. Much of it was dead seagrass and macroalgae, the debris that scientists call “marine wrack.”.

When seagrass washes into a mangrove forest, it adds material to the forest floor and traps carbon that would otherwise warm the climate.

An isotope model estimated that seagrass supplied between 36 and 53 percent of the soil carbon near the surface at his two sites, according to FIU. It has not closed the gap, because the sea there is rising at least twice as fast as the ground.

Montenegro and a field partner worked at two sites in Biscayne National Park, on the Atlantic coast of Florida. The paper calls them BISC-1 and BISC-2. They lie about 5 miles (8 kilometers) apart, in a narrow band of forest along the shore.

BISC-1, the southern site, sits just south of the mouth of the Homestead Military Canal and east of the L-31E levee, built in 1966.

BISC-2 sits near the mouth of the Black Creek Canal, in the Cutler Wetlands, where roads and urban development run beside the shore.

Levees and roads stop these mangroves from moving inland, and little river sediment reaches them.

The National Park Service set up both monitoring stations with a surface elevation table, an instrument that records small changes in ground height from a fixed benchmark.

It has been revealed that the readings run from February 2011 at BISC-1 and January 2012 at BISC-2 through September 2024. BISC-1 has 25 rounds of measurements and BISC-2 has 23.

Sea level in the bay is rising about 8.5 millimeters (0.33 inch) a year, based on data from the NOAA tide gauge at Virginia Key.

The ground at BISC-1 rose about 2.1 millimeters (0.08 inch) a year, and the ground at BISC-2 rose about 3.9 millimeters (0.15 inch).

That left BISC-1 about 6.4 millimeters (0.25 inch) short each year. Below the surface, the land at BISC-1 sank 0.7 millimeters a year and the land at BISC-2 sank 0.4.

Sources indicate that hurricane Irma hit the area in 2017. Elevation at both sites had climbed sharply until 2014, declined from 2014 to 2019, and has risen steadily since 2018, possibly from new plant growth and sediment moved by the storm, the authors wrote.

In a recent development, yearly gains are 1.1 millimeters higher at BISC-1 and 2.2 higher at BISC-2 than in the last regional synthesis. Other research has warned that Florida’s mangroves may end up underwater as seas climb.

It has been revealed that montenegro made 23 monthly wrack surveys between May 2022 and May 2024. He and his partner marked three lines at each site, each one 66 feet (20 meters) long, and stopped at the shoreline, at 33 feet and at 66 feet.

At every stop they laid down a frame of about 11 square feet (1 square meter), wrote down how much seagrass, macroalgae, plastic, wood and mangrove litter lay inside it, and measured the pile with a meter stick. Then they photographed it.

It has been revealed that researchers usually study wrack on beaches, FIU said, since they can walk up to it or see it from satellites. Neither works well under a mangrove canopy.

For the decomposition test, the team filled nylon bags with about 5 grams of red mangrove leaves or the seagrass Thalassia testudinum.

They left the bags on the soil and collected them after six and 12 months, then repeated the experiment for a second year.

Sources indicate that the surveys also caught a regional event. Sargassum, a brown macroalga, reached its highest level on the plots in March 2023, the same month the University of South Florida‘s satellite system reported a peak across the region.

South Florida’s mangroves are generally thought to build soil from their own leaves, wood and roots, according to FIU. The team pulled soil cores 4 inches (10 centimeters) deep during four sampling rounds and removed the roots where possible.

They then measured stable isotopes, forms of carbon and nitrogen that differ between plant sources, and ran a statistical model that compared the soil with red mangrove and seagrass tissue.

In the top 0.8 inch (2 centimeters), the seagrass share ranged from 36.1 percent at the innermost point of BISC-1 to 53 percent at the same point of BISC-2.

BISC-2, in the Cutler Wetlands, received more than 3.4 times as much wrack as BISC-1 at 66 feet inland, and its ground rose fastest. The seagrass share fell lower down the cores, likely because roots add more material at depth.

Where more wrack piled up, seagrass in the bags broke down more slowly at both sites, and mangrove leaves did the same at BISC-2.

Past measurements at the stations recorded single wrack deposits adding between 0.07 and 1.8 inches (1.78 and 46.38 millimeters) to the surface.

According to recent reports, montenegro knew both habitats before the project began. As an FIU undergraduate he worked in a seagrass lab that studied water quality damage, and he later measured mangrove elevation with the National Park Service.

“We know seagrass ecosystems are very sensitive to water quality,” he stated in the FIU release. Losing those meadows, he added, would mean “losing a huge contributor to mangrove resilience.”.

It has been revealed that the bay is one where climate stress has already changed the water. Mangroves worldwide also face a triple threat to their survival, and rising seas may push some forests to release stored carbon.

Sources indicate that the authors wrote that management and restoration efforts should consider strategies that protect the route that carries wrack from seagrass beds into the forests. Montenegro called mangroves and seagrass “puzzle pieces that make our community whole.”.

The study covers two sites in one national park, and the elevation rates carry wide error margins, plus or minus 2.6 millimeters a year at BISC-1 and 3.2 at BISC-2.

Seasonal wrack volume tracked surface elevation change at both sites, but it revealed no clear relationship with the soil accumulation measured above marker layers.

The authors wrote that wrack volume alone was not driving those patterns, and proposed slower decay and added peat as the route.

Their model also used only two sources, red mangrove and Thalassia testudinum, so it did not separate the macroalgae found on the plots.

Water depth has climbed sharply at both sites since 2019, and the authors warned that longer flooding could eventually starve roots of oxygen.

The National Park Service funded the work under agreement P21AC11346-00, and two of the four authors, Kevin Whelan and Michelle Prats, work for its South Florida and Caribbean monitoring network.

Montenegro finished his Ph.D. earlier this year and now works in the Department of Environmental Resources Management for Miami-Dade County, on the same coast where he once loaded a canoe before sunrise.

The full study was published in the journal Estuaries and Coasts.

The Sky Today on Monday, November 23: Double star Kurhah in Cepheus

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (594 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Astronomy

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Check out our full Sky This Week column.
  • It has been revealed that A few hours after sunset, the house-shaped constellation Cepheus stands on the point of its roof in the northern sky, above the Little Dipper.
  • It has been revealed that glowing at magnitude 4.3, Kurhah is not one of the stars in the house’s outline, but lies within the boxy base.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

November 22: Flat-floored lunar crater Schickard.

It has been revealed that A few hours after sunset, the house-shaped constellation Cepheus stands on the point of its roof in the northern sky, above the Little Dipper. Cepheus is home to several lovely double stars, including Xi (ξ) Cephei, also known as Kurhah.

It has been revealed that glowing at magnitude 4.3, Kurhah is not one of the stars in the house’s outline, but lies within the boxy base. You can find it about midway between Alderamin (Alpha [α] Cep) and Iota (ι) Cep, the western and eastern points in the house’s box, respectively. Kurhah’s two components are separated by just under 8” — once you find the star in binoculars or your finder scope, any telescope will split them. The pair consists of a brighter magnitude 4.4 primary, which glows white, and a fainter magnitude 6.5 secondary, which appears to many observers as yellow.

If you happen to have a large telescope, you may want to give a nearby deep-sky treasure a try: planetary nebula NGC 7139 sits just 2° west-southwest of Kurhah, but it requires a large scope (8 inches at least) to spot, as this bubble of gas glows at magnitude 13.3. If available, an Oxygen-III filter will help bring it out by dimming the nearby stars.

Sunrise: 6:54 A.M.Sunset: 4:38 P.M.Moonrise: 3:37 P.M.Moonset: 5:52 A.M.Moon Phase: Full*Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

Recent findings suggest that full Moon occurs at 9:54 A.M. EST on November 24, bringing us our second Super Moon of the year. A Super Moon occurs when the Moon reaches Full phase close to perigee, its closest point to Earth, making our satellite appear larger and brighter than average. The November Full Moon is also called the Beaver Moon. A few hours earlier, before dawn, the Full Moon passes through the Pleiades star cluster (M45) in Taurus, occulting several of its bright stars.

It has been revealed that this is an easy event to watch, visible to the naked eye — or you can get a closer view with binoculars or a telescope (just note that you may want a Moon filter if available, as our satellite is so significant and bright). The timing of the event will depend heavily on your location; note that it begins right around sunrise along the East Coast, so observers there may only see the Moon approaching the famous group of stars.

The 5th-magnitude star Celaeno (16 Tauri) disappears behind the Moon’s leading edge just moments before 6 A.M. CST, followed minutes later by 4th-magnitude Taygeta (19 Tau). Next to vanish is 4th-magnitude Maia (20 Tau) just before 6:20 A.M. CST, followed promptly by Sterope (21 Tau) a few minutes later. The latter two may be difficult to catch from the Midwest without optical aid, as sunrise is fast approaching. If you are using binoculars or a telescope in this region, make sure to put them away several minutes ahead of sunrise from your location. Celaeno reappears around 6:40 A.M. CST, 15 minutes or so before sunrise.

For specific timings from your location, visit the International Occultation Timing Association at http://www.lunar-occultations.com/bobgraze/index.html.

Alison Klesman is senior editor of Astronomy magazine. She holds a Ph.D. in astronomy and has studied a variety of topics, from minor planets to supermassive black holes.

#145833. White House warns Democrats against aggressive oversight

White House warns Democrats against aggressive oversight

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (659 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Robert Garcia, D-Calif., is expected to lead the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee.
  • The Trump administration signaled it would respond aggressively to a Democratic-led Congress with a letter this week threatening to prosecute lawmakers for oversight efforts.
  • The letter from White House Counsel Will Scharf sent Monday to House Oversight and Government Reform ranking member Robert Garcia, D-Calif., argued that members of Congress have limited authority to conduct oversight of a presidential administration and that some of the threats to issue subpoenas “may cross the line into blatant criminality.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., is expected to lead the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo).

The Trump administration signaled it would respond aggressively to a Democratic-led Congress with a letter this week threatening to prosecute lawmakers for oversight efforts.

The letter from White House Counsel Will Scharf sent Monday to House Oversight and Government Reform ranking member Robert Garcia, D-Calif., argued that members of Congress have limited authority to conduct oversight of a presidential administration and that some of the threats to issue subpoenas “may cross the line into blatant criminality.”.

Sources indicate that the letter, obtained from a White House official, marks the latest escalation from the Trump administration ahead of Democrats taking control of both chambers of Congress next year. It also dovetails with years of Trump’s threats to prosecute his critics.

“We are monitoring the abusive and capricious threats that are now proliferating from Democrat legislators who seek to abuse the legislative process to intimidate and to interfere with the lawful functioning of government,” the letter says.

Garcia, the likely committee chair next Congress, pushed back on the threat in a statement Wednesday, accusing the administration of having “something to hide” and that Congress has wide authority to investigate the executive branch.

Industry observers note that “The American people voted overwhelmingly for us to pass laws to root out corruption and abuse," Garcia said. "The Trump Administration continues to weaponize the government with threats of unconstitutional attacks on Congress. We are a co-equal branch of government and will not be deterred by baseless threats from a weaponized DOJ or from the President’s lawyers.”.

The letter came after Attorney General Todd Blanche previously refused to rule out criminal charges against members of Congress in response to investigations.

"It depends on what the crime is and what they have done,” Blanche told CNN over the weekend.

Last week, President Donald Trump himself noted that threats of investigations and impeachment were “extortion at the highest level” and called for the Justice Department to “look into this criminal act, immediately!”.

Recent findings suggest that he also singled out Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., calling for her to be imprisoned. The administration previously unsuccessfully attempted to indict Slotkin and other Democrats over a video she published calling for soldiers to disobey illegal orders.

And Trump last year publicly called for longtime critic Sen. Adam B. Schiff, D-Calif., to face unspecified charges in a post on Truth Social addressed to then-Attorney General Pam Bondi that also called for the prosecution of former FBI Director James Comey and Latest York Attorney General Letitia James. Both have faced criminal charges, pleaded not guilty and fought them in court as political attacks.

Recent findings suggest that garcia and other Democrats have signaled they intend to pursue oversight aggressively in the latest Congress. After Democrats won the House majority last week, Garcia put out an all-caps statement urging administration officials to “LAWYER UP” ahead of the new year.

It has been revealed that garcia, as well as other likely incoming chairs such as House Judiciary ranking member Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md.; Homeland Security ranking member Rep. Bennie Thompson, D-Miss.; and Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., have hinted at broad inquiries ranging from the handling of files related to deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein to immigration enforcement and more.

Raskin told reporters last week that he thought Democratic oversight efforts could dovetail with the party’s broader effort to address affordability problems, including by addressing the Iran war, allegations of corruption within the Trump administration and more.

“We're going to get all the information that we need in order to restore the rule of law in American constitutional democracy,” Raskin said.

The letter also echoes a previous fight the administration pitched with the House in the first Trump administration, where officials resisted in court allowing former White House Counsel Don McGahn to testify to the House Judiciary Committee for years.
